The following type of secondary glaucoma occurs as a consequence of central vein occlusion:
explanation_verbatim: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) can lead to retinal ischemia and release of VEGF, promoting new vessel growth on the iris and angle, causing neovascular (rubeotic) glaucoma.

stem: The classical treatment of congenital glaucoma:
The classical treatment of congenital glaucoma:
explanation_verbatim: The definitive treatment for congenital glaucoma is surgical (e.g., goniotomy or trabeculotomy). Medical therapy offers only temporary pressure reduction before surgery.

stem: Sign of primary open angle glaucoma:
Sign of primary open angle glaucoma:
explanation_verbatim: In primary open-angle glaucoma, the optic disc shows a large cup-to-disc ratio due to progressive loss of nerve fibers. Other findings include raised IOP and visual field defects.

A 55-year-old patient came to the clinic with frequent changes of the reading glasses. On examination, the visual acuity was 6/6 and the intraocular pressure was 28 mmHg in both eyes. Fundus examination showed a hemorrhage on the optic disc of the right eye and the cup to disc ratio was 0.8 in both eyes. Which of the following investigations is useful to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Automated perimetry assesses visual field loss typical of glaucoma. It confirms the diagnosis suggested by elevated IOP and optic disc cupping.

stem: The normal range for IOP as measured by applanation tonometry is:
The normal range for IOP as measured by applanation tonometry is:
explanation_verbatim: The normal intraocular pressure (IOP) measured by applanation tonometry ranges between 10 and 21 mmHg. Values outside this range may indicate glaucoma or ocular hypotony.

stem: A 55-year-old patient presents with gradual, painless diminution of vision. Examination reveals an intraocular pressure of 31 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows optic disc cupping. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?

A 55-year-old patient presents with gradual, painless diminution of vision. Examination reveals an intraocular pressure of 31 mmHg. Fundoscopy shows optic disc cupping. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
explanation_verbatim: Open-angle glaucoma with high intraocular pressure and optic disc cupping is treated surgically by trabeculectomy, which creates a new drainage pathway. It lowers IOP to prevent further optic nerve damage.

stem: The trabecular pathway is responsible for what percentage of aqueous drainage?
The trabecular pathway is responsible for what percentage of aqueous drainage?
explanation_verbatim: About 90% of aqueous humor drains through the trabecular (conventional) pathway into Schlemm’s canal. The remaining 10% drains via the uveoscleral (unconventional) route.

stem: Which fibers are most resistant to glaucomatous damage?
Which fibers are most resistant to glaucomatous damage?
explanation_verbatim: In glaucoma, the superior and inferior arcuate fibers are damaged first, leading to visual field loss in the corresponding areas. The papillomacular bundle, which carries fibers from the macula to the optic disc (central vision), is most resistant to glaucomatous damage and usually affected only in late stages.

stem: A 60-year-old patient presents for routine eye examination. Visual field testing shows peripheral field defects. Intraocular pressure is elevated at 30 mmHg, and fundoscopy reveals optic disc cupping. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 60-year-old patient presents for routine eye examination. Visual field testing shows peripheral field defects. Intraocular pressure is elevated at 30 mmHg, and fundoscopy reveals optic disc cupping. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Elevated IOP, optic disc cupping, and peripheral field loss are classic features of chronic open-angle glaucoma. It is usually asymptomatic until late stages.

stem: A 65-year-old patient presents with sudden onset severe eye pain, nausea, and seeing colored halos around lights. On examination, there is ciliary injection, a cloudy cornea, and a mid-dilated vertically oval non-reactive pupil. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 65-year-old patient presents with sudden onset severe eye pain, nausea, and seeing colored halos around lights. On examination, there is ciliary injection, a cloudy cornea, and a mid-dilated vertically oval non-reactive pupil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_verbatim: Sudden painful red eye, halos around lights, and mid-dilated pupil are hallmarks of acute angle-closure glaucoma. It is an ophthalmic emergency requiring immediate treatment.

Which of the following is the best line of management of a diabetic patient presenting with acute angle closure glaucoma together with lower limb edema and dyspnea?
explanation_verbatim:
Medical treatment of acute angle closure glaucoma (to lower IOP, reduce pain, and clear corneal oedema in preparation for iridotomy).
Topical medications: IOP lowering drugs (previously mentioned), miotics & Prednisolone.
Systemic medications: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (for IOP lowering) & Osmotic agents: Mannitol (contraindicated in cardiac patients) and glycerine (contraindicated in diabetics).

A patient with iridocyclitis was found to have WBC clumps on the back surface of the cornea. Which of the following might occur as a complication of that condition?
explanation_verbatim: Anterior uveitis can be complicated by 2ry glaucoma, Posterior synechiae, Complicated cataract, Calcific band keratopathy (if the iritis becomes chronic) especially in juvenile idiopathic arthritis & Macular oedema (if the iritis becomes chronic).
